issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette: Mary, an 80-year-old woman of Oceania descent, has been a welder for most of her life. She is married and has spent decades working in a bustling workshop environment where she was known for her precision and skill with metal. However, her life took a dark turn several years ago when her husband began to abuse her physically. The trauma began subtly at first but gradually escalated into severe beatings that left Mary bruised and broken. She had come to believe that her body had been permanently damaged by these assaults - her joints ached, her limbs moved stiffly, and she felt perpetually on edge. The physical abuse was not the only wound; it also cut deep into her emotional core, leaving her feeling numb and disconnected from any sense of normalcy. The nightmarish events played out against the backdrop of her daily routine at work and home. Her husband's unpredictable temper meant that Mary never knew when he would lash out again. This constant fear manifested in her sleep patterns: she found it increasingly difficult to fall asleep, often lying awake for hours worrying about whether she was safe. Once asleep, she would wake up abruptly during the night, convinced something was wrong and needing to check if her husband had come home or if there were any signs of danger. Mary's feeling of physical vulnerability extended beyond just her sleep disturbances; it permeated her daily life at work. As a welder, Mary's job required precision and trust in her body's movements. Now, she felt that she could no longer rely on herself to perform tasks as efficiently or safely as before. This doubt led her to avoid certain projects that she had previously excelled at, causing a noticeable decline in her productivity. Her husband's abuse also affected her relationships with colleagues, who began to notice her withdrawal and reduced performance. Mary's fear of being hurt again made it difficult for her to trust anyone fully, even those she had worked alongside for years. This isolation deepened over time as she withdrew from social interactions both at work and in her personal life. The cumulative effect of these experiences was a profound sense that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. Mary's ability to connect with others emotionally suffered greatly; she found it hard to laugh, cry, or even experience joy. The trauma had left her feeling like an outsider in her own skin and life. Mary's husband eventually moved out after years of abuse, but the fear and vigilance did not dissipate. Even inside her home, Mary felt on guard at all times. She would check locks repeatedly, keep a phone nearby for emergency calls, and avoid certain areas of the house where she had been hurt most severely. These behaviors further isolated her from her husband and friends. It was during one particularly brutal night when she woke up several times to ensure everything was safe that Mary finally decided to seek help. Her sleep problems had become so severe that they were affecting every aspect of her life, including her ability to perform even basic tasks at work. What frightened her most was the realization that if things continued this way, she would lose not only her job but also any sense of normalcy in her daily routine. Mary came into therapy hoping for a return to some semblance of stability and peace. She was certain that her body had been permanently damaged by what happened, but she also harbored a glimmer of hope that with help, she could regain trust in herself and reconnect emotionally with those around her. The fear that kept her awake every night was matched only by the desire to reclaim a life where she felt safe and able to live without constant vigilance.
